WIC28A-01.explanation: "Cowed" fits: the pack killed few elk, yet the herd stopped lingering in the thickets, stayed watchful while feeding, and kept doing so even when the wolves were thirty miles off, so the wolves changed the herd's behavior through fear. "Chased" fails because the elk avoided the thickets in weeks when no wolf was near them, so no pursuit was pushing them out. "Ambushed" fails because most kills were on the open benches, away from the thickets that could have hidden a wolf. "Corralled" fails because the elk fed in scattered bands across the benches, so they were spread out rather than confined.

WIC28A-02.explanation: "Cemetery" fits: young voles settle in the strip, and owls hunting from the poles kill more than half of them there within a month, so the strip is where the voles die. "Corridor" fails because the voles stop within a few hundred yards of where they enter and are killed there within weeks, so they do not pass along it. "Cage" fails because voles can wander back to a woodlot, so the strip does not hold them in. "Cafeteria" fails because, although the voles feed on its seed, over half of them are killed there by owls within a month, so what the strip mainly does to them is kill them, not feed them.

WIC28A-03.explanation: "Clinic" fits: fish take turns hanging still while the outcrop's shrimp crawl over them and into their mouths, and where the shrimp were removed groupers rub themselves against the sand, which shows the shrimp had been ridding them of something that irritates them; the outcrop is where reef fish go to be cleaned. "Canteen" fails because the visitors hang motionless with mouths open while shrimp work on them; the visitors are being tended, not eating. "Bedroom" fails because the visits are by day and end within minutes. "Ballroom" fails because the groups are of mixed species, each fish hanging alone in its turn, with no courtship.

WIC28A-04.explanation: "Chilled" fits: the turbines release water from the bottom of a deep reservoir, and below the dam trout have replaced bass, which now live only thirty miles downstream, so the river below has turned cold. "Bled" fails because the gravel bars lie as deep under water as before 1960, so the river below carries as much water as ever; the bass left for another reason. "Churned" fails because the release is even day and night, and the only surge is the river's own snowmelt flood spilling over in May, not anything the turbines do. "Clogged" fails because that flood still rolls the gravel bars every year, so silt and plants cannot settle and choke the channel.

WIC28A-05.explanation: "Boycotted" fits: the wool was being shipped from the port in record amounts, yet it disappeared from the alliance's markets, so the alliance had stopped buying from the port. "Blockaded" fails because freighters loaded more wool than ever and the port had its busiest year, so ships came and went freely. "Bombarded" fails because the waterfront sheds were filling and emptying with record cargoes, so the waterfront was working. "Annexed" fails because the island's council still appointed the harbormaster.

WIC28A-06.explanation: "Bulldozed" fits: within a year the church's ground was a parking lot and its stones were broken up and laid under a road, so the council had it knocked down. "Condemned" fails because condemning is a declaration that a building is unfit, and the council went much further, tearing down a church its engineers had found sound and breaking up its stones. "Crated" fails because stones broken small and spread under a road were never packed to be rebuilt. "Commandeered" fails because the council made no use of the church building; it cleared it away and used the ground.

WIC28A-07.explanation: "Capsized" fits: the squall laid the three ships' masts flat on the water, and their crews clung all night to the barnacled keels, which means the hulls had turned bottom up; the weather overturned them. "Beached" fails because this happened in mid-channel and the crews had to be picked up by other ships, so there was no shore near. "Becalmed" fails because the ships were struck while carrying full sail in a squall, so they had more wind than they could bear. "Blinded" fails because ships a mile off watched the three lanterns go down, so the crews could see.

WIC28A-08.explanation: "Banquet" fits: hundreds of scavengers crowded onto the carcass at once and ate it all within months, one huge feast that ended when the flesh was gone. "Cupboard" fails because nothing was kept back to draw on later; the crowd consumed all of it in four months. "Battery" fails because the bones were finished within a year, so the carcass gave up its energy in a burst rather than slowly over a long time. "Bridge" fails because the scavengers are the kinds of animals that turn up at any bait on that seafloor, so the carcass linked no populations that were apart.

WIC28B-01.explanation: Flowers the birds could not reach dropped whole without setting fruit, while nearly every flower a bird had probed set fruit, so the birds "pollinated" the tree. "Patrolled" fails because the birds spent their visits head-down in the blossoms and caterpillars chewed netted and open leaves alike, so the birds kept no insects off. "Propagated" fails because the fruit falls unopened beneath the tree, where the seedlings come up, so the birds carry no seed anywhere. "Parasitized" fails because the nectar the birds drink is repaid: without them the tree sets no fruit at all.

WIC28B-02.explanation: The falcons took mostly old birds and birds crippled by string, and with fewer mouths at the crumbs more young survived, refilling the flock to its old count, so the falcons "rejuvenated" the flock, replacing old and lame birds with young ones. "Reduced" fails because the surviving young brought the count back to its 1996 level. "Redistributed" fails because the pairs kept to their old ledges. "Rattled" fails because the lowest pairs nested a few yards below the falcons, which unsettled birds would not do.

WIC28B-03.explanation: A celebrated actress recited the poems in sold-out halls across the country and cheap editions followed her from city to city, so her poems had been "popularized": carried to a wide public. "Pirated" fails because each cheap edition carried her printer's license and paid her share of every copy, so none was printed without leave. "Plagiarized" fails because the actress named the poet each night. "Panned" fails because the city papers had named two of the poems among the season's best.

WIC28B-04.explanation: The officers took the bronzes and big canvases under a signed list, melted the bronzes into cannon, hung the canvases in the commander's headquarters, and refused to sell them back, so the army had "requisitioned" the collection: seized it officially for its own use. "Ransacked" fails because the pieces were crated, numbered and signed for, not rifled. "Ransomed" fails because the council offered to buy the pieces back and the army refused. "Repatriated" fails because the pieces went to the army's foundry and headquarters, not to the towns they had come from.

WIC28B-05.explanation: The lines move through ingredients and then through stages of the same barley, sprouted and then crushed, with days of waiting beside the stages, and a second column doubles every amount, all under the brewer's seal, so the tablet is the brewer's "recipe": quantities and steps for a brew in two batch sizes. "Roadmap" fails because the days sit beside stages of one batch of barley, so the places named are only where the ingredients come from, not stops on a route. "Receipt" fails because a column that restates every amount at exactly twice the size sets out quantities to use, not goods someone acknowledged receiving, and the seal is the brewer's own. "Payroll" fails because no line names a person.

WIC28B-06.explanation: Each family drank from the spring, left a ribbon on a thorn hung with ribbons from earlier years, and carried its water home to the sick, so the walk was a "pilgrimage": a journey to a place held to be holy, made in devotion. "Roundup" fails because they walked home between the grazing ponies, leaving them where they were. "Pageant" fails because the ribbons were left on the thorn as offerings, and the water went to the sick, so the hats served a devotion, not a show. "Raid" fails because the neighboring parish visited the same spring on its own day, so the spring was shared, not taken from them.

WIC28B-07.explanation: Miners left watches, pistols and fiddles in the safe and received sums of money against them, then took them back for the sum plus a tenth or saw them priced for sale, so the store was the camp's "pawnshop": a lender against pledged goods. "Repository" fails because the goods were not simply kept for their owners: money was paid out against them, and unredeemed ones were put up for sale. "Pharmacy" fails because the bottles on the shelf held whiskey. "Parlor" fails because the stove room had no chairs, so it was where business was done, not where the camp sat together.

WIC28B-08.explanation: Softened asphalt was pressed a little lower each summer under trucks that always used the same wheel tracks, and by 1990 rain pooled for days in two long lines up the climb, so the surface had been "rutted": worn into grooves along the wheel paths. "Rippled" fails because folds come from braking trucks shoving asphalt forward, and at the stop sign, where they braked hard, the asphalt lay flat. "Raised" fails because the asphalt was pressed lower, not lifted. "Ruptured" fails because the rain stood in the grooves for days without draining away, so the asphalt beneath it held unbroken.

WIC28C-01.explanation: "Drugged" fits: tended aphids grew few wings and crept slowly, and untended aphids slowed the same way on leaves the workers had crossed, clipped and carried indoors, far from any ant, so something the ants leave on the leaves was restraining the aphids chemically. "Herded" fails because the restraint did not need the ants at all: aphids slowed on clipped leaves with no ant present, so it was a substance working on them, not ants gathering or steering a group. "Devoured" fails because the tended aphids multiplied all summer; their row ended with fewer only because its slowed, wingless aphids never spread to new plants. "Garnered" fails because the aphids were never collected anywhere: they went on multiplying out on the plants.

WIC28C-02.explanation: "Gnawed" fits: a plank that looks smooth outside, apart from pencil-lead holes, weighs almost nothing and crumbles, so creatures have eaten the wood away from within. "Entombed" fails because the current sweeps the sand off the hull every tide, leaving it exposed. "Encrusted" fails because the barnacles are on the spilled slates, while the plank's own surface came up pale and smooth. "Dismantled" fails because the hull's outline can still be traced from keel to rails; the planks are sagging where they are, eaten hollow, not broken apart and scattered.

WIC28C-03.explanation: "Hearth" fits: the bricks on the wall's sunny face hold heat into the night, and the peaches trained against them set fruit in springs when frost kills the blossom everywhere else, so the wall is the orchard's source of warmth. "Fence" fails because the wall runs along one edge only and is open at both ends, so it closes nothing in or out. "Dike" fails because the river runs past the orchard's southern edge while the wall stands on its northern edge, with the trees between them, so the wall cannot hold the river off the orchard. "Firebreak" fails because the village lies across the river, and when it burned, the fire stopped at the water; it never came near the wall on the orchard's far side.

WIC28C-04.explanation: "Dump" fits: the museum sent down works it had struck from its catalog and could not even sell, its inventory marks them destroyed, and the chamber was walled up and never reopened, so the mine was where it got rid of them. "Depository" fails because a depository keeps things for their owner to retrieve; these works had been struck from the catalog, so the museum no longer counted them as its own, and its inventory now marks them destroyed, so they were put away for good rather than held for later. "Hospital" fails because the water-stained copies were leaned against the walls and bricked in, with no one ever working on them. "Gallery" fails because, although the paintings were set out in rows along the walls, the chamber was bricked up at once and has stayed shut, so no one ever saw them.

WIC28C-05.explanation: "Dried" fits: the ivy's leaves overlap like shingles, and after a week of rain the stone behind them was pale and powdery while the bare stone was soaked a foot deep and growing moss, so the ivy kept the wall dry. "Fortified" fails because the bare half, in the same sound mortar, came through the gale just as well, so the ivy added no strength. "Dislodged" fails because the gale took no stone from the ivy half. "Etched" fails because the rootlets leave the stone unmarked when pulled away.

WIC28C-06.explanation: "Denuded" fits: where grass and heather hide the ground on the ungrazed slope, the grazed one shows stones and bare earth between a few short tufts, and its soil washes into the stream with every storm, so the flock has stripped the hillside of its cover. "Groomed" fails because grooming keeps a cover neat; here the cover itself is mostly gone, leaving bare ground between scattered tufts. "Fertilized" fails because the droppings are washed downhill by the next rain before they break down, so they never enrich the slope. "Furrowed" fails because the sheep drift over the whole slope as they feed, so they wear no lines into it.

WIC28C-07.explanation: "Doctored" fits: the print reproduces the survey exactly except at the navy's own harbor, where its channel runs over rock and invented shoals block the real one, on a chart sold in quantity to foreign captains, so the engraver falsified the survey at the one place where misleading other navies mattered. "Flipped" fails because the print lies over the survey line for line, compass rose included, so nothing is reversed. "Enlarged" fails because a print that matches the survey line for line on a light table is drawn at the survey's own size. "Gilded" fails because the only things the print adds are two shoals across a real channel, which change the chart's facts rather than dress it up.

WIC28C-08.explanation: "Dredged" fits: mud full of the creek's own pebbles lies heaped on the banks, and the pools are three feet deeper than in the creek next door, so the beavers have scooped out their creek's bed. "Flooded" fails because they build no dams and the creek's surface stands where old survey stakes put it; the extra depth is below the water, not over the land. "Deforested" fails because aspens still shade both banks. "Greened" fails because by midsummer its grass browns with the rest of both valleys.

WIC28D-01.explanation: Nine days of water sank steadily down through loose sand, and corn given the same fertilizer as the higher field came up pale and short, so the flood had "leached" the field, carrying its nutrients down out of the roots' reach. "Manured" fails because equal fertilizer produced weaker corn on the flooded field than on the dry one, so the flood took food from the soil rather than adding it. "Mulched" fails because the water ran clear from a reservoir, carrying no litter to lay down, and by June the wind was lifting the bare sand off the rows, which no covered field allows. "Mired" fails because, wet as the sand still was, the water had been draining down through it and the corn went in on schedule.

WIC28D-02.explanation: The ebbs carry the marsh's shredded grass into the cove, and the shrimp grow fastest just where those stems settle, so the marsh is the bay's "kitchen": the place where its animals' food is made. "Kidney" fails because the water left with all the creek's fertilizer, so the marsh removed none of that waste. "Net" fails because the marsh sends material out rather than catching it: the water left as brown with mud as it came, now carrying the stems too. "Lung" fails because the cove below it runs short of oxygen as the marsh's stems rot there, so what the marsh sends the bay uses oxygen up rather than supplying it.

WIC28D-03.explanation: The dunes buried the caravan road forty feet deep, so the village could be reached only by a three-day walk over their crests, while its families went on living in a hollow among them: the sand had "imprisoned" it, shutting it in. "Lifted" fails because, though the way in now runs forty feet above the old road, the village's own doorways still open at their builders' height, so the sand rose around the village, not under it. "Nibbled" fails because the families kept every house and date garden; the dunes took the basin around the village, not pieces of the village. "Lashed" fails because the village lies in a still hollow below dunes taller than its palms, sheltered from the wind that would drive sand against it.

WIC28D-04.explanation: Residents of the two neighborhoods the yard divided came in equal numbers on the same evenings and stayed two hours, and friendships between them rose from one tower family in twenty to one in three, so the park is the district's "mixer," where the two communities come together. "Magnet" fails because the park draws no more visitors than the city's other parks of its size; what sets it apart is not how many it pulls in but the friendships formed among those who come. "Junction" fails because a junction is where ways meet and cross, and these visitors stay two hours at the fields and market; what the park changed is how the people in it relate, which is mixing. "Muffler" fails because the lawns slope open to the highway, leaving nothing to absorb its noise.

WIC28D-05.explanation: The ice was frozen to the ground and left the meadows' old soil in place, while its own meltwater, driven along its base under pressure, cut a slot two hundred feet deep into the granite, so the glacier left the floor "incised": cut by a narrow channel and otherwise untouched. "Milled" fails because ice frozen fast to its bed does not slide and grind, and the soil with pollen older than the ice survived under it. "Mantled" fails because the question is what the glacier left: the ice that lay over the floor is gone, the meadows' surface is the old soil, and all the rock it carried went into the ridge at the valley's mouth, so nothing was left covering the floor. "Littered" fails because that rock lies heaped in one ridge at the mouth, not strewn across the meadows.

WIC28D-06.explanation: The editors met weekly with the war ministry, ran its recruiting appeals and casualty lists free, and the papers' own peace writer turned to urging readers to enlist, so the government "mobilized" the press, enlisting it in the war effort. "Muzzled" fails because the peace columns stopped when their own writer changed sides, and no official saw a page before it ran, so the press was recruited, not silenced. "Nationalized" fails because the founding families still owned the papers and paid for the added pages. "Impoverished" fails because those families paid out of profits that climbed with wartime sales.

WIC28D-07.explanation: Sand dropped by the current covered the ship to its masthead within a decade, and the survey team had to pump away twelve feet of it to reach the deck, so two centuries of seawater had "interred" the ship, burying it. "Mummified" fails because the timbers had gone soft and black, so the sand kept the hull's shape and kept out the worms without preserving its wood as it was. "Mined" fails because the shipworms that riddle every exposed wreck on that coast never reached these buried timbers, which were solid through. "Jostled" fails because the hull lay on its side exactly as it first struck, its slate still stacked, so the strong current had covered it rather than moved it.

WIC28D-08.explanation: The translator moved the story to an English village, turned its fjord into an estuary and its money into shillings, and gave every character an English name, so he "naturalized" the novel, making it at home in English life. "Lightened" fails because every drowning and every winter of hunger is told in full, so the book is as grim as before. "Mutilated" fails because he kept every chapter, cutting nothing. "Manicured" fails because his sentences keep the original's short, abrupt rhythm clause by clause, so he did not smooth the author's style.

WIC28E-01.explanation: The swells broke along the bar while boats moored behind it at the piers survived storms that wrecked boats on the open coast, so the bar sheltered the harbor from the sea: a "seawall." A "tollbooth" is a point where everyone passing must pay, but ships steered over without a pilot along publicly buoyed water, so crossing cost them nothing. A "turnstile" admits traffic one at a time, but ships crossed several abreast on every high tide. A "wharf" is where cargo is loaded and unloaded, but the ships crossed the bar and unloaded at the town's piers.

WIC28E-02.explanation: No tree was lost, yet afterward the pines grew slowly for a decade and let in beetles that a healthy pine drowns in resin, so the drought left them weakened: it "sapped" the forest. "Winnowed" means sifted out the weaker part, but every tagged tree survived, and the beetles settled in large and small trees alike, so nothing was sorted out. "Scorched" means burned or browned, but the needles grown in the dry summers lasted their usual three years. "Toppled" means brought down, but every tree tagged in 1952 still stood in 1975.

WIC28E-03.explanation: Each stretch of the river held stones of nearly one size, and painted stones traveled with each flood to wherever the bed held stones their own size, so the river had separated its stones by size along its course: it had "sorted" them. "Stacked" means set one on another, but the painted stones moved on with every flood. "Stained" means colored from outside, and the spring does run orange, but the orange runs clear through any stone cracked open, so it is the rock's own color. "Sanded" means worn down by grit, and the river at the mouth carries grit, but broken pebbles there still fit back together edge to edge.

WIC28E-04.explanation: Melting only in sunlight and draining down bare rock, the glacier makes the river rise every summer evening and fall before dawn, and the mills start at the evening rise, so it marks the time of day: it is the valley's "timepiece." A "storeroom" holds supplies for later, but its water passes within a night and the ditches draw on springs. A "thermometer" registers temperature, but its front stood at the same ledge in the frozen 1810s and the hot 1860s. A "signpost" points travelers along a route, but though it is visible from every village, it lies under cliffs that no road or path crosses.

WIC28E-05.explanation: The daughter standardized the mother's spelling, broke her run-on lines into sentences, restored skipped small words and fixed dates the mother herself had corrected, changing how the diary was written but not what it said: she "tidied" it. "Tightened" means made more concise, but the book has four hundred more words than the notebooks. "Softened" means toned down, but the quarrels read more evenly only because of the new punctuation, with every curse still in place. "Spliced" means joined in material from elsewhere, but the redated entries are the mother's own, moved according to her own penciled corrections.

WIC28E-06.explanation: A stream that fell through riffles and cascades above the mill was backed into a half-mile pond that a floating leaf took an hour to cross, so the mill calmed its current: it "stilled" the stream. "Siphoned" means drew water away, but the whole stream spilled over the wheel and ran on down its old bed. "Walled" means hemmed in by built banks, but apart from the dam the pond lay between reedy margins that cattle grazed down to. "Soured" means fouled the water, but trout rose every evening in the pond where the wool was rinsed.

WIC28E-07.explanation: Twenty-eight men were aboard, none reached the island or its beaches, and the hatches were still battened in 1960, so the crew's remains are sealed inside: the hull is a "tomb." A "strongbox" keeps valuables secure, and the holds are sealed, but they hold only coal. A "trellis" is a framework growth depends on, but the growth on the hull is part of one growth covering the reef for a mile each way. A "tripwire" catches passing ships, but the bow lies ninety feet down while the freighters overhead draw twenty.

WIC28E-08.explanation: Wine was poured at the gate, and in most years what drovers and merchants on the road paid came to more than the rent from its fields, so the monastery made its living serving drink to travelers: it was the valley's "tavern." A "sanatorium" takes in the sick to recover, but the townspeople who came for weeks each September were paid by the day to pick grapes. A "scriptorium" is where books are written out, but its three hundred books were bought at the city fairs. A "vault" keeps valuables safe, but its chests were emptied each spring to pay for a new chapel.
